Aerial Wildlife 
Survey Report 
Wildlife Management Unit 357 Aerial Ungulate Survey - 2015 
 
Background 
For the years of 2000 to 2006 there was a consecutive period of unusually mild winters which promoted high 
ungulate survival and recruitment rates, resulting in rapid population growth. In response to this growth there was 
growing concern related to the depredation of crops by ungulates. We increased the number of licences and 
hunting opportunities across the WMU, and implemented multiple tags per licence for both species of deer to 
address these concerns. Following several winters with deep snow and colder te mperatures recent public 
perceptions of declines in both mule and white-tailed deer have precipitated concerns over the health of ungulate 
populations. The objectives of this survey were to assess the status of moose, white -tailed deer, mule deer and 
elk populations since the last survey in 2009, determine a population estimate, population ratio for sex and age 
classes, and a density estimate for moose and deer within Wildlife Management Unit 357.  
 
Survey method 
Distance sampling methods were used to determine population estimates for moose and deer. Sampling 
transects were generated by constructing a grid of rectangles (1.2 km by 10 km) oriented north -south. We 
selected a simple random sample of rectangles, and surveyed the centerline of these rectangles. The survey was 
flown as described in the Distance Sampling Chapter of the Aerial Ungulate Survey Protocol Manual (ESRD, 
2014). Elk populations are highly clumped and traditional sampling methods do not reliably estimate elk densities. 
Therefore elk observed during the distance sampling transects were classified and counted and an additional 
separate survey for elk was flown to determine minimum total counts. This elk survey focused on areas that were 
not surveyed during the transects in areas where elk herds were known to occur, with high quality habitat, or 
areas with recent complaints regarding elk damage. 
 
Results 
One hundred and forty seven transects were surveyed on January 5-16, 2015 for a total survey effort of 1289 km 
and 33.4 hrs flying time. An additional 14.9 hrs flying time were allocated to elk surveys. In total, 202 moose were 
observed from 132 independent groups of moose. Of the 202 moose that were successfully classified, 47 (23%) 
were bulls, 115 (57%) were cows, and 40 (20%) were calves. Of the bulls observed, 49% had  already shed their 
antlers. Of those bulls still with antlers, 60% were small and 40% were medium. No large bulls were observed. 
The bull:cow and calf:cow ratio were 0.41 and 0.35, respectively. The final density estimate was 0.362 
moose/km2 with a log-based 90% confidence interval of (0.288, 0.455) and a CV of 13.9%. The estimated moose 
abundance for WMU 357 is 2514 (90% CI 1999, 3160).

In total, 236 mule deer were observed from 46 independent groups of mule deer. Of the mule deer detected there 
were 51 bucks (22%), 126 does (53%) and 59 fawns (25%). The buck:doe and fawn:doe ratio were 0.40 and 
0.47, respectively. The final density estimate was 0.380 mule deer/km2with a log -based 90% confidence interval 
of (0.244, 0.590) and a CV of 27.2%. The estimated mule deer abundance for WMU 357 is 2634 (90% CI 1695, 
4095). 
 
In total, 239 individuals were observed from 69 groups of white-tailed deer. Of these individuals, 31 were bucks 
(13%), 139 were does (58%) and 69 were fawns (29%). The buck:doe and fawn:doe rati o were 0.22 and 0.50, 
respectively. The final density estimate was 0.595 white-tailed deer/km2 with a log-based 90% confidence interval 
of (0.405, 0.872) and a CV of 23.5%. The estimated white-tailed deer abundance for WMU 357 is 4128 (90% CI 
2814, 6056). 
 
A total of 1585 elk were observed, with a bull:cow and calf:cow ratio of 0.18 and 0.24, respectively. Note that this 
is a minimum population count of elk in this WMU.
